item.title: 2 Nov 2026: Britomartis Appendices
item.description:
Show her how it’s done, Artemis!

Of course, when I said I translated everything from antiquity concerning Britomartis, I meant in Greek. A few things I translated but didn’t include above:

  • Diodoros of Sicily, Library of History V 48–9, 76.3–77.2 (cf. Homeros, Ilias XX 215–240; Hesiodos, Theogoneia 969–74; Homeros, Odusseia V 125–8). (Note that Euboulos “of good counsel” is an epithet of Ploutos “wealthy,” cf. the Orphic Hymn to Ploutos and Hesukhios.) I didn’t include my translation above because it’s long and almost exclusively about Britomartis’s ancestors—not that this is without interest to the myth! just outside the scope of what I was posting about—though it does note that she was born at Kaino (from καίνω “to kill”).
  • Strabon, Geography X 4.12 is critical of Kallimakhos’s association of Mount Dikte with Diktunna, since the Kudonians (who are said to have raised an altar to her) live in the west of Crete, while Dikte is in the east, doesn’t overlook the sea, and was sacred to Zeus (being his birthplace—Dikte is usually taken to be from τίκτω “to give birth”); he suggests that perhaps Kallimakhos meant Mount Tituros, which is in fact in Kudonia and has a promontory overlooking the sea which was the site of the temple of Diktunna.
  • Various inscriptions engraved on altars, walls, etc. which reference Britomartis, Dictunna, etc. none of which are terribly interesting (except that they often list her alongside Artemis, corroborating accounts that the name refers to a hero in the retinue of Artemis rather than being a mere epithet of her).

I didn’t even look in Latin. This is because I tend to think poorly of Rome and, anyway, can’t read it. I recently found a couple Britomartis references in Latin, though:

  • Pseudo-Virgil, Ciris includes Karme (the mother of Britomartis) as a character and has a digression (283–309) where she laments the loss of her daughter and references the myth. This includes a few details not mentioned or in disagreement with elsewhere: Karme grieves the loss of Britomartis (like Tros over Ganumedes); Britomartis has a Parthian (e.g. recurve composite) bow (like the τόξον παλίντονον of Eurutos, cf. Odusseia XXI 11); Britomartis is punningly associated with the discovery of δίκταμνον diktamnon “dittany of Crete” (cf. Aristoteles, History of Animals IX 7.1; Virgil, Aeneid XII 411–5); Britomartis is believed to have fallen (rather than leapt) from the promontory into the sea; and Britomartis was said to have hounds (rather than girls) as companions (woof woof).
  • Servius on the Aeneid III 171 briefly recounts the Britomartis myth, calling her Dikte and associating Mount Dikte and dittany with her.

item.title: 26 Oct 2026: How Long do Demons Live?
item.description:
You know, I’ve only been really seriously studying this spirituality stuff for seven years or so, but it’s amazing what kinds of lore one picks up. My daughter asked me today if demons live forever, and of course (as material beings) they don’t, but then she asked me how long they lived for, and much to my surprise I had a ready answer for her:

ἐννέα τοι ζώει γενεὰς λακέρυζα κορώνη,
ἀνδρῶν ἡβώντων ἔλαφος δέ τε τετρακόρωνος
τρεῖς δ’ ἐλάφους ὁ κόραξ γηράσκεται αὐτὰρ ὁ φοίνιξ
ἐννέα τοὺς κόρακας: δέκα δ’ ἡμεῖς τοὺς φοίνικας
νύμφαι ἐυπλόκαμοι, κοῦραι Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο.

A screaming sea-crow* lives nine generations,
of boys reaching their prime, and a deer is four sea-crows,
and three deer the old age of a raven, but the phoenix
is nine of the raven, and ten phoenixes are we
well-braided maidens, the daughters of aigis-bearing Zeus.

  • sea-crow: an unknown species of small seabird.

(A neias speaking. Hesiodos, as quoted by Ploutarkhos on the Failing of Oracles §11.)

The first part was interpreted variously even in antiquity—Ploutarkhos has his characters argue over it—but it seems to me to mean that a sea-crow lives for nine generations in the time it takes for a boy to reach his prime. Hesiodos seems to place this around thirty (cf. Works and Days 695), but to make the math easy, let’s call it twenty-seven. In that case, it would make the sea-crow’s lifespan three years, a deer’s twelve (plausible), a raven’s thirty-six (also plausible), the phoenix’s 324 (cf. Herodotos’s 500), and a nymph’s 3240. Ploutarkhos notes that Pindaros says that nymphs live as long as trees, and we know some species, like bristlecone pines, Patagonian cypresses, and giant sequoias, that can attain to such an age.

My shoulder Thomas Taylor would like me to remind you that, in contrast, angels live perpetually and gods live eternally.

item.title: 25 Oct 2026: Circle Sibyl
item.description: An attempt at the face which appears in the Moon. I laid her out on a Flower of Life grid, using only circles with integer radii, in the hopes that she would be easy to construct using only a compass, but my best attempts so far have far too many inelegant auxilliary circles for my liking.

item.title: 22 Oct 2026
item.description:
Porphurios makes the point in his letter to his wife Marcella that, while it is difficult to force people to wear fetters of iron, if you give them the (much heavier!) fetters of gold, they will wear them willingly.

What would he think, I wonder, of the plastic and silicon fetters that people wear today?

item.title: 16 Oct 2026: Bouncy Castle
item.description:
οὐδὲν ἀκιδνότερον γαῖα τρέφει
Earth breeds nothing more pathetic than ἀνθρώποιο,
a human,

πάντων ὅσσα τε
of all the things that γαῖαν ἔπι
on Earth πνείει
breathe τε καὶ
and ἕρπει.
creep:*

οὐ μὲν γάρ ποτέ φησι
for he never expects κακὸν πείσεσθαι
to suffer misfortune ὀπίσσω,
later on

ὄφρ’
so long as ἀρετὴν παρέχωσι θεοὶ
the gods grant prosperity καὶ
and γούνατ’
his knees ὀρώρῃ:
move;*

ἀλλ’
but ὅτε δὴ
as soon as καὶ λυγρὰ θεοὶ μάκαρες τελέσωσι,
the blessed gods also bring about miseries,

καὶ τὰ φέρει
he bears these too, ἀεκαζόμενος
unwillingly, τετληότι
suffering θυμῷ:
at heart.

τοῖος γὰρ
For such νόος ἐστὶν
is the mind ἐπιχθονίων ἀνθρώπων
of earthbound humans:

οἷον
however ἐπ’ ἦμαρ
on a given day ἄγησι πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε.
the father of men and gods leads it.

  1. creep: cf. Ilias XVII 446–7.
  2. his knees move: that is, while he has strength.

(Homeros, Odusseia XVIII 130–7.)

This has been a tricky week for me, awakening with spirits bright one day and crushed the next. I was talking with a friend earlier who has been experiencing similarly, so perhaps it is something in the air... if you are also on the roller coaster, may you find evenness and peace.
